definition: Measurement is the comparison of a physical quantity with a standard unit.
SI units are internationally agreed standard units used to measure physical quantities.
Length is the distance between two points.
Mass is the amount of matter in an object.
Time is the duration between events or the interval during which an event occurs.
Temperature is a measure of the degree of hotness or coldness of an object.
Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge.
Amount of substance measures the quantity of particles in a substance.
Luminous intensity is the amount of visible light emitted by a source in a particular direction.
A scalar quantity has magnitude only and no direction.
A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction.
Distance is the total length of the path travelled by an object.
Displacement is the change in position of an object from its initial position to its final position with direction.
Speed is the distance travelled per unit time.
Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken.
Velocity is the rate of change of displacement with respect to time and has direction.
Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time taken.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time.
Uniform motion occurs when an object travels equal distances in equal intervals of time.
Uniform acceleration occurs when velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time.
For constant acceleration, the equations of motion relate initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, displacement and time.
For constant acceleration, displacement can be found using initial velocity, acceleration and time.
For constant acceleration, velocity, acceleration and displacement are related by this equation.
Free fall is motion in which gravity is the only significant force acting on an object.
Acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface is approximately 9.8 metres per second squared.
Force is a push or pull that can change the motion or shape of an object.
Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted upon by a net external force.
Newton's second law states that the net force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration.
Newton's third law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of motion.
Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object.
Normal force is the contact force exerted perpendicular to a surface.
Friction is a force that opposes relative motion or attempted motion between two surfaces.
The coefficient of friction is the ratio of frictional force to normal force.
Tension is the pulling force transmitted through a stretched string, rope or cable.
Momentum is the product of an object's mass and velocity.
Impulse is the change in momentum produced by a force acting over a time interval.
The law of conservation of momentum states that total momentum remains constant in an isolated system when no net external force acts.
Work is done when a force causes displacement in the direction of the force.
Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object because of its motion.
Gravitational potential energy is the energy possessed by an object because of its height above a reference level.
Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy and potential energy.
The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed but can be transferred or transformed.
Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
Efficiency is the ratio of useful output energy or power to input energy or power, usually expressed as a percentage.
Circular motion is the motion of an object along a circular path.
Angular displacement is the angle through which an object rotates about an axis.
Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement with time.
Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity with time.
Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration directed toward the centre of a circular path.
Centripetal force is the net inward force required to keep an object moving in a circular path.
Torque is the turning effect of a force about an axis or pivot.
An object is in rotational equilibrium when the net torque acting on it is zero.
Newton's law of universal gravitation states that every two masses attract each other with a force proportional to their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.
The gravitational constant is the proportionality constant used in Newton's law of universal gravitation.
A gravitational field is the region around a mass in which another mass experiences gravitational force.
Density is the mass contained per unit volume of a substance.
Pressure is the normal force acting per unit area.
Pressure at a depth in a liquid depends on the liquid density, gravitational acceleration and depth.
Pascal's law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions.
Buoyant force is the upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object.
Archimedes' principle states that an immersed object experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.
For steady incompressible fluid flow, the product of cross-sectional area and fluid speed remains constant.
Bernoulli's principle states that for steady ideal fluid flow, pressure, kinetic energy per unit volume and gravitational potential energy per unit volume are related by a constant total.
Simple harmonic motion is oscillatory motion in which acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed toward the equilibrium position.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement of an oscillating object from its equilibrium position.
Time period is the time required for one complete cycle of a periodic motion.
Frequency is the number of complete cycles or oscillations per second.
Angular frequency is the rate of change of phase of periodic motion.
Hooke's law states that within the elastic limit, extension is directly proportional to applied force.
Spring constant measures the stiffness of a spring.
Elastic potential energy is the energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object.
A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without net transfer of matter.
Wavelength is the distance between two corresponding points on consecutive waves.
Wave speed is the speed at which a wave disturbance travels through a medium.
In a transverse wave, particles of the medium oscillate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.
In a longitudinal wave, particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
Wave amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle from its equilibrium position.
Wave period is the time required for one complete wave cycle.
The principle of superposition states that when waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the sum of their individual displacements.
Interference is the phenomenon in which overlapping waves combine to produce reinforcement or cancellation.
Constructive interference occurs when waves combine to produce a larger resultant amplitude.
Destructive interference occurs when waves combine to reduce or cancel the resultant amplitude.
Diffraction is the bending or spreading of waves around obstacles or through narrow openings.
Resonance occurs when a system is driven at or near its natural frequency and produces a large amplitude.
Sound is a mechanical wave that requires a material medium for propagation.
Sound intensity is the power transmitted by a sound wave per unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
The Doppler effect is the apparent change in observed frequency caused by relative motion between a source and an observer.
Reflection is the bouncing back of light into the original medium after it strikes a surface.
Refraction is the change in direction of light when it passes from one medium into another.
Refractive index indicates how much the speed of light is reduced in a medium compared with vacuum.
Snell's law relates the angles of incidence and refraction when light passes between two media.
Critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is 90 degrees.
Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser medium to a less dense medium and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.
The mirror formula relates focal length, object distance and image distance for a spherical mirror.
Magnification is the ratio of image height to object height.
The lens formula relates focal length, object distance and image distance for a thin lens.
The power of a lens measures its ability to converge or diverge light.
An electromagnetic wave consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields and can travel through vacuum.
Heat is energy transferred between objects because of a temperature difference.
Temperature measures the thermal state or average kinetic energy of particles in a substance.
Specific heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one kelvin.
Latent heat is energy transferred during a change of state without a change in temperature.
Thermal expansion is the increase or change in dimensions of a substance due to an increase in temperature.
The ideal gas law relates pressure, volume, amount of gas and absolute temperature.
Boyle's law states that for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume.
Charles's law states that for a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
The first law of thermodynamics states that the change in internal energy equals heat supplied to the system minus work done by the system.
Electric charge is a physical property of matter responsible for electrical interactions.
Coulomb's law states that the electrostatic force between two point charges is proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.
Electric field is the force experienced per unit positive test charge.
Electric potential is electric potential energy per unit charge.
Potential difference is the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between two points.
Ohm's law states that current through a conductor is directly proportional to potential difference when physical conditions remain constant.
Electrical resistance is the opposition offered to the flow of electric current.
Resistivity is a property of a material that describes its resistance to electric current.
For resistors connected in series, the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances.
For resistors connected in parallel, the reciprocal of total resistance equals the sum of the reciprocals of individual resistances.
Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is transferred or used.
Electrical energy is the energy transferred by an electric circuit.
Kirchhoff's current law states that the total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it.
Kirchhoff's voltage law states that the algebraic sum of potential changes around a closed circuit is zero.
A magnetic field is a region in which a magnet, magnetic material or moving charge experiences a magnetic force.
Magnetic flux measures the magnetic field passing through a surface.
A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force.
Lorentz force is the force experienced by a charged particle in electric and magnetic fields.
Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force due to a change in magnetic flux.
Faraday's law states that the induced electromotive force is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage.
Lenz's law states that the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it.
A transformer transfers electrical energy between coils through electromagnetic induction and can increase or decrease AC voltage.
An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains the chemical properties of that element.
An electron is a negatively charged subatomic particle.
A proton is a positively charged subatomic particle found in the nucleus of an atom.
A neutron is a neutral subatomic particle found in the nucleus of an atom.
A photon is a quantum or packet of electromagnetic radiation.
Planck's constant is a fundamental constant relating the energy of a photon to its frequency.
The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a material when electromagnetic radiation of sufficient frequency falls on its surface.
Work function is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of a material.
Radioactivity is the spontaneous decay of unstable atomic nuclei with the emission of radiation.
Half-life is the time required for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.
Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus into smaller nuclei with the release of energy.
Nuclear fusion is the combination of light atomic nuclei to form a heavier nucleus with the release of energy.
Mass-energy equivalence states that mass can be converted into energy according to Einstein's equation.
Special relativity describes the relationship between space and time for observers moving at constant velocity and states that the speed of light in vacuum is invariant.
Dimensional analysis uses fundamental dimensions to check physical equations and relationships.
Accuracy describes how close a measured value is to the true or accepted value.
Precision describes how close repeated measurements are to one another.
Measurement uncertainty represents the range within which the true value is expected to lie.
